newsitem.title: GERMANY: German SPD urges Kohl to speed up tax reform.
newsitem.headline: German SPD urges Kohl to speed up tax reform.

text.p: Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD) have jumped on the tax reform bandwagon, challenging Chancellor Helmut Kohl to cut income taxes even earlier than his government intends.

The SPD plan, which commentators hailed on Tuesday as a smart tactical move in a mounting debate over Germany's heavy tax burden, urges lower tax brackets for wage-earners and fewer loopholes for the rich in 1998, a year earlier than Kohl wants.
Even the Free Democrats, Kohl's liberal coalition partners who also want tax reform in 1998, welcomed the plan even though they favour deeper cuts for business and the better off.
"I'm very pleased the SPD is now moving on tax policy," FDP general secretary Guido Westerwelle told ARD television.

The SPD plan, approved by the party executive on Monday, aims to help its blue-collar clientele by cutting the starting tax rate to 19.5 percent from 25.9 percent and boosting the standard personal deduction from 12,000 marks ($8,066) to 14,000.
It would also close many of the countless loopholes clever tax advisors use to lighten the tax load for the wealthy.
The proposal came after a month of verbal brawling in Bonn between the FDP and Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) over the date for the long-awaited reform.

The SPD pointedly left open the issue of lowering the peak tax rate of 53 percent, saying it still had to see how much new revenue was needed from higher-bracket taxpayers to help make up for the 50 billion marks lost through the reform.
"I don't want to talk about a peak rate because that depends on how many loopholes we can close," SPD finance expert Ingrid Matthaeus-Meier told the Sueddeutsche Zeitung.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel has already said Bonn wants to cut the minimum tax rate to around 20 percent and drop the ceiling to under 40 percent. The government plan would also close loopholes, although none have been identified so far.
But Waigel, who has already warned the FDP not to press for an early reform, insists Kohl's coalition will not agree on the details of its plan until late this year.
It should be passed into law during 1997 but not take effect until after the general election planned for late 1998.

Kohl has said Germany probably had to raise value-added tax sometime in future but promised this would not happen before 1999. VAT is currently 15 percent on most items and both the FDP and the SPD are firmly against raising it.
Handelsblatt, Germany's business daily, said the SPD had succeeded in taking the initiative in the tax debate.
"All other tax plans presented in the coming months will have to judged in comparison to these SPD proposals," the newspaper wrote in an editorial entitled "Tactical Advantage."
"That goes especially for the tax proposals of the Bonn coalition due at the end of this year," it wrote.
Munich's liberal Sueddeutsche Zeitung also saw the plan as a clever move to put pressure on Kohl to speed up tax reform.
"There is no procedural reason for a delay," it wrote. "All that is needed now is political courage, but that's up to the government because it will be responsible for the result."
While welcoming the SPD's move, Westerwelle said the plan would not result in any real drop in an overall tax burden the FDP sees as a brake on initiative and investment.

"We now have an overall tax rate of 46 percent," he said. "We have to cut this in real terms. The best thing would be to get back within this decade to an overall rate of 40 or 41 percent, like we had before German unity (in 1990)."
